newsitem.title: USA: U.S. officials expect problems in Bosnia elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials expect problems in Bosnia elections.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Friday they expected "some disruptions" in Bosnian elections on Saturday, but pledged to work with whomever was elected to move the Balkan peace process forward.

A senior official of the National Security Council said it was hard to imagine that the elections could be perfect after 40 years of Yugoslav communist dictatorship and four years of ethnic war in Bosnia.

"There will inevitably be some disruptions and some problems," said Alexander Vershbow, NSC senior director for European affairs. "But we have succeeded in creating the conditions in which we think that balloting can go forward."

The elections are the climax of a U.S.-sponsored peace process begun by last year's Dayton peace accord, which created a two-part Bosnian state composed of a Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb republic.

Critics have charged that the elections are likely to confirm in power strongly nationalist parties from all ethnic groups who are likely to intensify the partition of Bosnia rather than create a unified state.
But Vershbow told a briefing: "One can't decide that an election shouldn't be held just because one isn't entirely happy with the results."
At the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "We're going to sit down with those people who've been elected to convince them to implement the election."

He conceded that these might include Serbs and others suspected of complicity in war atrocities, but said: "We will do it because peace and securing peace is the most important objective that we have."

Burns compared Bosnia to Germany following the Second World War. "At some point you've got to make the decision to let the local population run their own affairs. And that's the decision that we've made in Bosnia," he told reporters.
U.S. officials said representatives of the major powers would want to meet Bosnia's elected leaders as soon as possible after the elections, although no date had yet been fixed.
One key decision for Washington and its allies is what, if any, peacekeeping operation to mount in Bosnia after the mandate of the current NATO-led implementation force, IFOR, expires on Dec. 20.

Vershbow said a meeting of NATO defence ministers in Norway at the end of this month would make an early assessment of the elections, but other officials said no decision on an IFOR follow-on force is expected until later in the year.

The question is politically sensitive in the United States because of presidential elections on Nov. 5. President Bill Clinton has pledged that the nearly 20,000 U.S. troops in IFOR will leave Bosnia by the end of the year.
But Kofi Annan, U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, said on Friday he saw a "general consensus developing that there will have to be continued military presence after December."
He told reporters in Washington that the United Nations would not be involved in such a force, although it would continue to engage in police training and strengthening the legal system.
